newsitem.title: USA: Strike at WHX not just over pensions-USW.
newsitem.headline: Strike at WHX not just over pensions-USW.

text.p: The two-day old strike at WHX Corp is not only about pensions and wages, but also about health-care issues and language that would eliminate union jobs by contracting them out, United Steelworkers union officials said Wednesday.
"This is not just a pension and wage question," said Jim Bowen, the union's chief negotiator with WHX, parent of Wheeling-Pittsburgh Steel Corp in Wheeling, W.Va.

Some 4,500 workers struck Wheeling-Pittsburgh Steel on Tuesday after their former contract expired and negotiations failed to produce a new one. The strike has affected eight steel plants in three states. No talks are scheduled.
Company officials were not available for comment.
At a news conference, Bowen said the company wants to contract out services that would eliminate jobs among office and clerical workers, track repair workers and plant nurses.
He said the company also wants union members to pay 20 percent of their medical bills out of the existing health-care network and to increase workers' out-of-pocket medical expenses by 66 percent.
Bowen said the pension dispute is the major divisive issue. The company currently has a defined contribution plan, which is funded based on the number of hours an employee has worked.

The union wants a defined benefit plan, which guarantees funding regardless of hours worked. "(The company) has told me that until the union is ready to meet and accept their pension proposal, there is no need to meet," Bowen said.

Until this year, the company was barred by a bankruptcy ruling from offering a defined benefit plan. The company wants to enhance the existing defined contribution plan and has maintained it cannot afford a defined benefit plan.

"They definitely can afford this," Bowen said, adding the company has $400 million of cash in hand. "If (WHX Chairman Ron LeBow) would spend between one-quarter and one-third of that money, he could take care of the pension problem this afternoon."

The company proposed monthly retirement benefits of $1,200 to $1,600, plus a $1,000 bonus. Bowen called that proposal inadequate, noting that only about 15 percent of the 4,500 workers would be covered by it.

Bowen played down industry rumors that LeBow would use the strike as a means to close plants or sell off portions of the steel company. "What would (a buyer) do, buy a strike?" he said. "If (LeBow) could find an idiot like that, he probably would sell it."
"It doesn't make any difference how long this thing may last," said Mickey Forte, president of Local 1187. "We're not going to settle this until we get the pension we feel we deserve."
Short-term, the strike is not expected to have much effect on the steel market. But if it drags on, some industry analysts feel the tightened supply will boost prices at other steelmakers.
